title: Routers and static routes
summary: Join two networks through a router. Learn why traffic needs a route there and a route back.

tasks.title: Reach the far side of the router
tasks.text: From **client**, `ping 10.12.2.254` (the router's DMZ address) says `Network is unreachable`. Give the client a route so this ping works.
hints: Look at `ip route` on the client. It only knows its own network, `10.12.1.0/24`.
The router's address on the client's network is `10.12.1.254`. That is the next hop.
`ip route add default via 10.12.1.254` (or a specific route: `ip route add 10.12.2.0/24 via 10.12.1.254`).

tasks.title: Fix the way back
tasks.text: The client can now reach the router's far side, but `ping 10.12.2.10` (the server) gets no reply. The request arrives; the reply has nowhere to go. Fix it on the **server**.

checks.fail_msg: client still gets no reply from 10.12.2.10.

hints: Open a shell on the router and run `tcpdump -ni any icmp` while pinging from the client. You will see requests going out and nothing coming back.
The server needs a route to `10.12.1.0/24`. Its router address is `10.12.2.254`.
On server: `ip route add default via 10.12.2.254`.

tasks.title: Trace the path
tasks.text: Run `traceroute -n 10.12.2.10` from the client. What is the IP address of the **first hop**?
hints: The first numbered line of traceroute output is hop 1: the first router on the path.

tasks.title: Use the network
tasks.text: The server runs a web site on port 80. Fetch it from the client with `curl` and submit the flag it shows.
